sections.section_title: The Jerusalem Visit — Revelation, Not Summons
sections.summary: Paul narrates his revelation-prompted visit to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, where the uncircumcised Greek Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, and Paul refused to yield to false brothers who sought to spy out the believers' freedom in Christ and reduce them to slavery.

The recognized Jerusalem leaders — James, Cephas, and John — added nothing to Paul's gospel, recognized the grace given to him, extended the right hand of fellowship, and agreed to a division of labor with Paul going to the Gentiles and the pillars to the circumcised, asking only that Paul remember the poor.

Paul publicly opposed Cephas at Antioch because Cephas, who had been eating with Gentile believers, withdrew under pressure from men associated with James, and his hypocrisy spread to the other Jewish believers and even Barnabas, effectively forcing Gentile believers to Judaize in contradiction of the gospel's truth.

sections.section_title: The Thesis Stated — Justification by Faith, Not by Proselyte Conversion
sections.summary: Paul states the letter's central thesis — that no one is justified by works of the law (circumcision and proselyte conversion) but through faith in Christ Jesus — three times in a single sentence, then develops it through a series of declarations: rebuilding the demolished law-system makes the rebuilder a transgressor, Paul died to the law and was crucified with Christ, his life is now lived by faith in the Son of God, and if righteousness came through the law then Christ died for no purpose.
sections.relevance: While the primary argument concerns the basis of justification (faith vs. law-works) rather than its permanence, the passage carries significant implications for conditionality. Verse 18 states that if a believer who has been justified by faith rebuilds the law-covenant system as a basis for justification, that person 'proves himself to be a transgressor' — post-justification conduct affects standing. Verse 21 declares 'I do not nullify the grace of God,' with the verb atheteo ('to set aside, to annul') implying that grace can be nullified by those who return to law-works as a justification basis. This theological framework is the direct foundation for the explicit conditionality warning in 5:4 ('you have fallen from grace'). The ongoing nature of living 'by faith' (v. 20) also suggests faith must be maintained, not merely initiated. Against this, the decisive, completed character of being 'crucified with Christ' (perfect tense, v. 19) and the relocated identity ('Christ lives in me,' v. 20) carry implications of permanence, creating genuine tension within the passage.
key_phrases: a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ
